subtype: Approach: hypothesis testing with one change at a time [Thinking]
passage: Thursday, 1 am, finally quiet. The site went slow tonight, so I wrote my guess on a sticky note first: the pool of database connections has run dry. If that's true, raising the pool size a little should ease things. Changed only that. Waited ten minutes and watched the graph: waiting requests dropped, but errors stayed. So the guess was partly right, not the whole story. I didn't touch the timeout or the cache at the same time, even though Keerthana pinged, 'just try everything?' Next idea: a slow query hogging connections. One change again, a limit on that query, and the errors stopped. Notes are in the incident doc so the morning shift can see the order I tried things. Tired, pleased. — Kalyani

qa.q: What did Kalyani write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Kalyani wrote a guess that the pool of database connections has run dry.

qa.q: How does Kalyani feel at the end of the night?
qa.a: Kalyani feels tired but pleased, having found the fix by changing one thing at a time. 🙂

qa.q: What could Kalyani do if a single change showed no result at all?
qa.a: Kalyani could ask a second engineer to compare the graphs from before and after, since fresh eyes may spot a pattern the first guess missed.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see the one-change-at-a-time method?
qa.a: Keerthana may find it slower than trying everything, but would likely value it later, since the notes show which change helped.

grounding: Shows an engineer stating a guess about the connection pool, testing it with one change, observing the result and only then moving to the next idea.

passage: I'm Rekha, and that night I was the one on the status page. Every thirty minutes I posted a short update: what we knew, what we didn't, and when the next one would come. Zubin, who was leading the fix, sent me two lines at a time and I turned them into plain words. The first update said only, 'Payments are slow, we're looking into it, next update at nine forty.' Not glamorous, but at nine forty I posted again, even when the news was 'still working on it'. What surprised me was the support inbox. It had been flooding, and after the third update the messages slowed. One customer wrote, 'Thanks for actually telling us.' I was nervous the whole time, but I learned that people can bear bad news better than silence.

qa.q: How often did Rekha post an update?
qa.a: Rekha posted an update every thirty minutes.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel during the outage?
qa.a: Rekha was nervous the whole time, though the customer thanks brought some relief. 🙂

qa.q: What other approach could Rekha add if the cause stayed unknown for hours?
qa.a: Rekha could also message the biggest customers directly, since a public page may not be enough for people who depend on the service most.

qa.q: How might a customer have felt after reading the third update?
qa.a: A customer would likely feel calmer and respected, since one wrote 'Thanks for actually telling us.'

grounding: Shows a communications owner posting short honest updates on a regular schedule with the next update time, which eased customer worry.

subtype: Approach: hero engineer who refuses help [Pitfall]
passage:
Ayesha: Indu, it's been five hours. Want me to take the logs for a bit?
Indu: I've got it. Explaining would take longer than doing it.
Ayesha: Then at least sleep an hour. I'll page you.
Indu: No. Almost there 🙂
[two hours later]
Indu: oops
Indu: I ran the wrong command on the live database. It needs a restart from scratch.
Ayesha: Okay. Don't touch anything else. I'm calling the on-call lead now.
Indu: sorry. I should have handed over hours ago 😔
Ayesha: Send me exactly what you ran. We'll sort it.
[The site stayed down until morning.]

qa.q: What did Indu do that lengthened the outage?
qa.a: Indu ran the wrong command on the live database.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling in the last messages?
qa.a: Indu felt regretful and embarrassed, apologising and admitting that a handover was due hours earlier. 😔

qa.q: What could Indu have done differently?
qa.a: Indu could have handed over the logs and rested, since a rested teammate might have caught the mistake or avoided it.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt when Indu turned down help?
qa.a: Ayesha was probably worried and a little sidelined, having offered twice and been refused.

grounding: Shows a senior engineer refusing help for hours until fatigue causes a wrong command that prolongs the outage.

passage: Two days after the outage, the team gathered in the small meeting room at the Hyderabad office with a whiteboard. Pankaj, who had pushed the release, sat with his arms crossed. Baljeet, leading the review, began, 'We're here to ask what let this happen, not who.' They built the timeline first: the deploy at 6:10, the first errors at 6:25, the customer report at 7:05. Then the causes. No alert had fired for the failing payments, and the rollback had never been tested, so it took forty minutes to work out. Pankaj uncrossed his arms and said, 'I should have tested it too,' and Baljeet answered, 'Then let's make the test part of every release.' Each action got an owner and a date: an alert, a rollback test, a checklist. The blame column stayed empty.

qa.q: Which two causes did the team find?
qa.a: No alert had fired for the failing payments, and the rollback had never been tested.

qa.q: What do Pankaj's crossed arms suggest at the start of the meeting?
qa.a: Pankaj was probably defensive and afraid of being blamed, and he relaxed once the review focused on the system.

qa.q: What could the team do to make sure the actions get finished?
qa.a: They could check the action list at the next team meeting, since owners and dates only help if someone looks at them again.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team have felt hearing 'what let this happen, not who'?
qa.a: They were probably relieved and more willing to speak honestly, since nobody had to fear punishment.

grounding: Shows a team writing a timeline, naming the missing alert and untested rollback as causes and assigning owned actions without blaming a person.

passage: I'm Bhavna, and I sat two desks from Tenzin the week after our long outage. Tenzin was quiet, the way people get when something has been bothering them. At Monday's meeting Tenzin suggested a drill: once a quarter we switch off one service in the test setup and practise our response steps. Some of us groaned. Tenzin didn't argue, just put a date in the calendar and asked me to help write the first scenario. The first drill was messy; we forgot who should call whom. By the third, people reached for the checklist without being told. I can't say whether Tenzin felt relieved or still worried, but the calendar entry for the next drill was there before anyone asked.

qa.q: How often are the drills held?
qa.a: The drills are held once a quarter.

qa.q: What might Tenzin have been feeling in the week after the outage?
qa.a: Tenzin was probably worried or unsettled, since Tenzin was quiet in the way people get when something has been bothering them.

qa.q: What could the team add to the drills, and why?
qa.a: They could rotate who leads each drill so everyone practises the commander role, since real outages do not wait for the usual person.

qa.q: How might the colleagues who groaned have felt by the third drill?
qa.a: They were likely more comfortable and confident, since by then people reached for the checklist without being told.

grounding: Shows a team scheduling regular failure drills in a test setting after an outage so that response steps become familiar.

passage: Come, sit, Minakshi, and I'll tell you about the worst night of my first job, and why I'm so strict about rest now. I'm Afreen, and I was incident commander for a banking outage. By hour six the engineers were snapping at each other, and I saw one of them type the same command twice. I thought: tired minds make mistakes, and mine is one of them. So I stopped, called a break, and sent home the two who had been up since midnight to sleep. Fresh people took over, and I handed my notes to a colleague and rested for three hours myself. Some said I was wasting time. When I came back, the new team had found the fault in twenty minutes. Since then I plan handovers before an incident starts.

qa.q: What had one engineer done by hour six?
qa.a: One engineer had typed the same command twice.

qa.q: What was Afreen thinking when seeing the repeated command?
qa.a: Afreen was worried that tiredness was causing mistakes, including Afreen's own, which is why Afreen stopped everything.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Calling a break and bringing in fresh people made the difference, since tired engineers were making mistakes and the new team found the fault in twenty minutes.

qa.q: How might the two engineers sent home have felt at first?
qa.a: They may have felt reluctant to leave in the middle of the crisis, but they were probably also relieved, having been up since midnight.

grounding: Shows a commander who, knowing tired minds make errors, rotates people and sends the first responders to sleep before returning.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: defining what AI may and may not do [Thinking]
passage:
'Let's decide before someone decides for us,' said Vijay, uncapping a marker. 'What can we use AI tools for?'
'Drafting test cases,' said Parul. 'Summarising public documents.'
'Yes. Also a first draft of release notes. What goes on the no side?'
'Anything with customer data.'
'Right. And passwords, keys, anything from the private repo pasted into a public tool. If I wouldn't pin it on a notice board outside, it doesn't go in.'
'What about code it writes?'
'Fine as a draft, but a person reads it before it merges. It can sound sure and be wrong.'
Parul wrote both lists on the whiteboard. 'It's clearer with a line down the middle,' she said. Vijay drew it, and they photographed the board for the group chat.

qa.q: Which two uses did Parul name as allowed?
qa.a: Parul named drafting test cases and summarising public documents.

qa.q: What does Vijay seem worried about at the start?
qa.a: Vijay seems worried that people will start using the tools in risky ways on their own, so Vijay wants a clear line agreed first.

qa.q: What other approach could help the rules stick?
qa.a: Vijay could put them on a short shared page and revisit it in a month, since tools and habits change quickly.

qa.q: How might Parul see the line down the middle?
qa.a: Parul finds it clearer, saying so, because two lists become a boundary the team can point to.

grounding: Shows a team lead listing the uses of AI tools that are allowed and those that are not, including keeping customer data and secrets out of public tools.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: writing a short usage policy [Action]
passage: On Thursday afternoon in a co-working space in Nairobi, Omar opened a blank page titled 'How we use AI tools' and asked Jin to write it with him. First came the tools the company had licensed. Second, data: no customer records, no keys, no unreleased plans. Third was a rule they argued over for ten minutes and kept: a person reads every AI-written change before it goes into the main code. They held it to one page and printed it, and Omar added a line asking people to say when AI had helped. On Monday, Jin slipped the page into the new-joiner pack. The next hire, a graduate called Wanjiru, read it over coffee and asked two questions that made them add a sentence.

qa.q: Which rule did Omar and Jin argue over for ten minutes and keep?
qa.a: They kept the rule that a person reads every AI-written change before it goes into the main code.

qa.q: What does Omar want from the extra line about saying when AI helped?
qa.a: Omar wants openness, so reviewers know which changes need a closer look, which shows care about the review rule.

qa.q: What could the team do to keep the policy alive?
qa.a: They could review the page every few months, since tools and habits change and a fixed page gets out of date.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru see the page in the first days?
qa.a: Wanjiru probably finds it helpful and short enough to read, since two questions led to one added sentence.

grounding: Shows a team writing a one-page guideline on approved tools, data handling and human review of AI-written changes, then sharing it with new joiners.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
passage: In the fifth-floor dev room of a logistics firm, Anjali, a junior developer, was rushing to clear a ticket before the evening stand-up. The AI tool wrote the search function in seconds, the tests turned green, and Anjali merged it without reading past the first lines. It felt like a small win. Three days later Sunaina, doing a routine pass over merged code, stopped at the query. It built its command by pasting user text straight into it, which left the search box open to tricks. Sunaina raised it with the team lead at once, the change was pulled, and the cleanup took two people a full day. Anjali sat very still at the stand-up. 'I just trusted that green meant fine,' she said quietly.

qa.q: How long after the merge did Sunaina notice the query?
qa.a: Sunaina noticed it three days later.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling at the stand-up?
qa.a: Anjali felt embarrassed and regretful, sitting very still and admitting a trust in green tests.

qa.q: What could Anjali do differently with AI-written code next time?
qa.a: Anjali could read every line, test odd inputs, and ask a colleague to review before merging, since passing basic tests does not prove the code is safe.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt on finding the query?
qa.a: Sunaina was probably concerned about the risk to users, which is why they raised it with the lead at once.

grounding: Shows a junior developer merging AI-written code unread, so an insecure query passes basic tests and reaches production before a reviewer notices.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: piloting on low-risk tasks first [Action]
passage: With one month left before an audit and no budget for extra hands, Nilesh proposed a small trial: use the AI tools only for documentation and first drafts of unit tests. Nikita, who had doubts about anything near the main code, agreed because of that limit. Each Friday they wrote down two numbers: minutes saved on a task and mistakes found in review. By week two the documentation drafts saved about a third of the time, though Nikita found a test that checked nothing. By week four the pattern was clear: good for docs, useful but needing care for tests. They put it on one page. Nilesh said the critical payment code would stay off limits until a longer trial, and Nikita, still cautious, nodded.

qa.q: Which two numbers did they write down each Friday?
qa.a: They wrote down minutes saved on a task and mistakes found in review.

qa.q: Why did Nikita agree to the trial?
qa.a: Nikita agreed because the limit kept the tools away from the main code, where Nikita had doubts, so Nikita was cautious but willing.

qa.q: What could Nilesh do to ease Nikita's doubts about the test drafts?
qa.a: Nilesh could ask Nikita to review the test drafts and log every weak one, since counting the flaws turns a worry into something measurable.

qa.q: How might a teammate who works on the payment code see the decision?
qa.a: A teammate would probably feel reassured, since the tools stay away from the payment code until a longer trial.

grounding: Shows a team trying AI tools on documentation and unit test drafts for a month, measuring time saved and mistakes, before considering critical code.
